subject: biology
title: Unit 4 summary and memory tips
summary: A condensed revision sheet for all of Unit 4: pathogens, innate and adaptive immunity, vaccines and emerging diseases, genetic change, speciation, fossils, phylogeny, human evolution and the practical investigation, plus memory tips.
body:
This revision sheet condenses all of VCE Biology Unit 4 into one set of notes: how organisms defend themselves against disease and how we fight outbreaks (Area of Study 1), how species change over time and how we know (Area of Study 2), and how to plan and present your own investigation (Area of Study 3). Read it through, test yourself on the questions, and return to the full lessons for any gaps.

## Area of Study 1a: Pathogens and the first line of defence

- A **pathogen** is an agent that causes disease. **Cellular pathogens**: bacteria (prokaryotes with a cell wall and 70S ribosomes), fungi, protozoa and worms. **Non-cellular pathogens**: **viruses** (nucleic acid in a protein **capsid**, sometimes an envelope; they replicate only inside host cells) and **prions** (misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid that make normal proteins misfold).
- Antibiotics act on bacterial structures, so they **do not work on viruses**.
- An **antigen** is a molecule that triggers an immune response. The body tolerates **self** antigens and responds to **non-self** antigens. An **allergen** is a harmless non-self antigen that triggers a response in some people.
- **MHC class I** markers are on **all nucleated cells**. **MHC class II** markers are only on **antigen-presenting cells** (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells).
- **First line of defence** (non-specific, stops entry):

| Type | Animals | Plants |
|---|---|---|
| Physical | Intact skin, mucous membranes, cilia, coughing | Waxy cuticle, cell walls, bark, closing stomata |
| Chemical | Lysozyme in tears and saliva, stomach acid, sebum | Antimicrobial and toxic chemicals |
| Microbiological | Normal flora outcompete pathogens | Beneficial microbes on roots and leaves |

## Area of Study 1b: The innate immune response (second line)

- **Innate** = rapid, non-specific, no memory.
- **Inflammation**: damage → **mast cells** release **histamine** → **vasodilation** (redness, heat) and **leakier capillaries** (swelling) → **chemotaxis** brings neutrophils, then monocytes that become macrophages → phagocytosis and repair. Pus = dead neutrophils, pathogens and fluid.

| Cell | Main job |
|---|---|
| Neutrophil | First and most common phagocyte; short-lived |
| Macrophage | Long-lived phagocyte from monocytes; releases cytokines; presents antigen on MHC II |
| Dendritic cell | Phagocyte that carries antigen to lymph nodes; links innate and adaptive immunity |
| Mast cell | Releases histamine |
| Eosinophil | Attacks large parasites (worms) by degranulation |
| Natural killer (NK) cell | Kills cells with reduced MHC I (virus-infected, cancer) by apoptosis using perforin and granzymes |

- **Complement proteins**: opsonisation (coat pathogens for phagocytes), chemotaxis, and lysis (punch holes in pathogen membranes).
- **Interferons**: released by virus-infected cells to warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication.
- **Fever**: **pyrogens** reset the hypothalamus to a higher temperature, which can slow pathogen growth and speed immune activity.
- **Lymphatic system**: returns tissue fluid to the blood; **lymph nodes** bring antigens and lymphocytes together.

## Area of Study 1c: Adaptive immunity (third line)

- **Adaptive** = specific, slower the first time, has **memory**. Uses **B cells** (mature in bone marrow) and **T cells** (mature in the thymus).
- **Antigen presentation**: a dendritic cell engulfs a pathogen, loads fragments onto **MHC II**, travels to a lymph node and presents to **helper T cells**. Infected cells display antigen on **MHC I** for cytotoxic T cells.
- **Clonal selection**: only the lymphocyte with the matching receptor is activated. **Clonal expansion**: it divides into many identical **effector cells** and **memory cells**.
- **Helper T cells** (CD4⁺) release **cytokines** that activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Losing them (as in HIV) weakens both branches.

| | Humoral | Cell-mediated |
|---|---|---|
| Main cells | B cells → **plasma cells** | **Cytotoxic T cells** (CD8⁺) |
| Target | Pathogens and toxins **outside** cells | **Infected** or abnormal body cells |
| Action | **Antibodies** | Perforin and granzymes cause apoptosis |
| Memory | Memory B cells | Memory T cells |

- **Antibody**: Y-shaped, 2 heavy and 2 light chains; **variable region** (two antigen-binding sites, specific to one **epitope**) and **constant region**. Functions: **neutralisation**, **agglutination** (clumping), **opsonisation**, **complement activation**.
- **Secondary response**: faster, larger and longer-lasting than the primary response, because memory cells are already present.

## Area of Study 1d: Vaccines, immunotherapy and emerging diseases

| | Active (own antibodies, memory) | Passive (given antibodies, no memory) |
|---|---|---|
| Natural | Catching the disease | Antibodies across the placenta or in breast milk |
| Artificial | Vaccination | Antibody injection, e.g. antivenom, monoclonal antibodies |

- **Vaccines** trigger a safe primary response so memory cells give a fast secondary response later. Types: live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, toxoid, mRNA, viral vector. **Boosters** strengthen memory.
- **Herd immunity**: when enough people are immune, transmission chains break, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.
- **Monoclonal antibodies** (hybridoma technology): mouse plasma cell (makes antibody) + myeloma cell (divides forever) = **hybridoma**; screen and clone. Uses: mark or block cancer cells, deliver drugs, **checkpoint inhibitors**, and dampen autoimmune disease (e.g. block TNF). They give passive immunity, so doses must be repeated.
- **Emerging diseases** are new or rapidly increasing; **re-emerging diseases** return after being controlled. Causes: mutation, **antigenic drift** (small, gradual changes) and **antigenic shift** (sudden swap of gene segments, pandemic risk), antimicrobial resistance, falling vaccination, environmental change.
- **Zoonoses** spread from animals to humans (sometimes via **vectors** such as mosquitoes). **Globalisation and air travel** spread pathogens fast, often during the incubation period.
- **Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples** have long-standing knowledge of plant-based medicines. Research should involve consent, acknowledgement and benefit sharing.
- **Controlling outbreaks**: surveillance, testing, contact tracing, finding the source, quarantine and isolation, vaccination, vector control, hygiene.

## Area of Study 2a: Genetic change in populations

- **Gene pool** = all alleles in a population. **Evolution** = change in **allele frequencies** over generations.
- Allele frequency = copies of that allele ÷ total copies of the gene (2 per diploid individual).
- **Mutation** is the only source of **new** alleles.
- **Natural selection** (non-random): variation exists → **selection pressure** → individuals with advantageous phenotypes survive and reproduce more → advantageous alleles are passed on more → their frequency rises.
- **Genetic drift** (random): chance changes, strongest in small populations. **Bottleneck effect** (sudden population crash) and **founder effect** (small group starts a new population) both reduce diversity.
- **Gene flow**: movement of alleles between populations; makes them more similar.
- **Selective breeding**: humans are the selection pressure; reduces genetic diversity.
- **Antibiotic resistance**: random mutation gives resistance; antibiotic use kills susceptible bacteria; resistant bacteria survive and multiply.

## Area of Study 2b: Speciation

- **Species** (biological species concept): can interbreed in nature to produce **viable, fertile** offspring.
- Speciation needs **gene flow to stop**, then different mutations, selection pressures and drift change each population's allele frequencies until they become **reproductively isolated**.
- **Allopatric** speciation: populations separated by a **geographical barrier**. **Sympatric** speciation: in the same area, e.g. **polyploidy** in plants.
- **Isolating mechanisms**: **pre-zygotic** (geographical, temporal, behavioural, ecological, structural, gametic) and **post-zygotic** (hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility such as the mule, hybrid breakdown).
- **Galápagos finches**: adaptive radiation from a common ancestor, with beaks suited to different foods on different islands.

## Area of Study 2c: Fossils, phylogeny and human evolution

- Fossils usually form after **rapid burial** in low-oxygen sediment; the record is **incomplete**. Types: petrified, moulds, casts, imprints, trace fossils, preserved remains.
- **Relative dating**: **law of superposition** (lower layers are older) and **index fossils** (widespread, short-lived species).
- **Absolute (radiometric) dating**: age = number of half-lives × half-life. **Carbon-14** (half-life about 5730 years) for organic remains up to about 50 000 years; **potassium-40** for very old volcanic rock. Fossils in sedimentary rock are dated from volcanic layers above and below.
- **Transitional fossils** show features of two groups, e.g. *Archaeopteryx* (reptile and bird).
- **Homologous structures** = common ancestor, different functions (divergent evolution). **Analogous structures** = same function, different origin (convergent evolution). **Vestigial structures** = reduced remnants.
- **Molecular homology**: fewer DNA or amino acid differences = more recent common ancestor. The **molecular clock** estimates divergence time. mtDNA is maternal, does not recombine and mutates quickly.
- **Phylogenetic trees**: nodes are common ancestors; relatedness is judged by the **most recent shared node**, not by how close tips sit. A **clade** is an ancestor and all its descendants.
- **Hominins**: humans and extinct relatives after the split from chimpanzees (roughly 6–7 million years ago), defined by **bipedalism** (central foramen magnum, S-shaped spine, bowl-shaped pelvis, angled femurs, arched feet). Trends: larger brain, flatter face, smaller teeth, more complex tools and culture. The tree is **bushy**. Evidence supports an **African origin** of *Homo sapiens* with interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans.

## Area of Study 3: Practical investigation and poster

- Write a focused, testable **research question** and a **hypothesis** with a biological reason.
- Change one **independent variable**, measure one **dependent variable**, keep **controlled variables** constant, include a **control** group and **replicates**.
- Consider **safety** and **ethics**; record everything in your **logbook**.
- **Random errors** are reduced by repeats; **systematic errors** shift every result the same way and need a better method or calibrated equipment. **Accuracy** = closeness to the true value; **precision** = closeness of repeats to each other.
- The **scientific poster** has a title, introduction, method, results, discussion and a conclusion that answers the question.

## Tips to remember

- **Three lines of defence = a castle**: the walls and moat (first line), the guards who attack anyone (second line), and trained snipers with a wanted list (third line).
- **MHC "1 for all, 2 for the presenters"**: MHC I on all nucleated cells; MHC II only on antigen-presenting cells.
- **Signs of inflammation "Red, Hot, Swollen, Sore"**: redness and heat from vasodilation, swelling from leaky capillaries, pain from pressure on nerves.
- **"B for Blood-borne antibodies, T for Touch-to-kill"** (made-up memory trick): B cells act through antibodies in body fluids; cytotoxic T cells must touch infected cells to kill them.
- **Helper T cells are the coach**: they don't score goals themselves, but without them neither team (B cells or cytotoxic T cells) plays well.
- **Antibody functions "NAOC" — "No Alien Organisms Can stay"** (made-up memory trick): **N**eutralisation, **A**gglutination, **O**psonisation, **C**omplement activation.
- **Active vs passive**: active = you **made** it (memory); passive = you were **handed** it (no memory, short-lived). Think "active is homemade, passive is takeaway".
- **Hybridoma = "a factory that never closes"**: plasma cell (the factory's product) + myeloma cell (never stops working).
- **Drift is a little drift, shift is a big lift**: antigenic drift = small gradual changes; antigenic shift = sudden swap of segments, pandemic risk.
- **Evolution needs "VISTA"**: **V**ariation, **I**nheritance, **S**election pressure, **T**ime, **A**daptation. (A common revision acronym for natural selection.)
- **Drift is like a lucky dip**: who happens to survive is chance, not fitness, and small bags give the most surprising results.
- **Allopatric = "other homeland"** (allo = other, patric = homeland); **sympatric = "same homeland"**.
- **Pre-zygotic stops the date; post-zygotic ruins the kids.** Pre-zygotic mechanisms prevent fertilisation; post-zygotic ones make hybrids die or be infertile.
- **Half-life halving**: 1 → 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8 → 1/16. Count the halvings, multiply by the half-life.
- **Superposition = a laundry basket**: the clothes at the bottom went in first.
- **Homologous = same "home" (origin); analogous = same "act" (function).**
- **On a tree, "follow the branches back to the nearest fork"**: the most recent shared node shows who is closest; ignore how close the names sit.
- **Bipedal skeleton "FSPFA" — "Five Steps Prove Feet Are used"** (made-up memory trick): **F**oramen magnum central, **S**-shaped spine, **P**elvis bowl-shaped, **F**emurs angled in, **A**rched feet.

## Summary

- The body defends itself in three lines: barriers, a rapid non-specific innate response, and a specific adaptive response with memory.
- Antigen presentation, clonal selection, helper T cells, antibodies and cytotoxic T cells drive adaptive immunity; vaccines and monoclonal antibodies use it to prevent and treat disease.
- Emerging diseases arise through mutation, antigenic change, zoonoses and travel, and are controlled by breaking transmission chains.
- Evolution is change in allele frequencies through mutation, natural selection, drift and gene flow; new species form when gene flow stops and populations diverge.
- Fossils, dating methods, structural and molecular evidence and phylogenetic trees reveal relationships, including the bushy history of hominins.
- A good investigation has a testable question, controlled variables, replicates, honest error analysis and a clear poster.

questions.prompt: Which pathogen contains no nucleic acid?
questions.explanation: Prions are misfolded proteins with no DNA or RNA. Option B is tempting because viruses are also non-cellular, but every virus contains DNA or RNA inside its capsid.

questions.prompt: A virus-infected liver cell displays viral antigen. Which marker does it use, and which cell recognises it?

options.A: MHC class I; cytotoxic T cell
options.B: MHC class II; helper T cell
options.C: MHC class II; cytotoxic T cell

questions.explanation: All nucleated body cells present internal antigens on MHC I, which cytotoxic T cells recognise. Option B is tempting, but MHC II is found only on antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes early inflammation?

options.B: Histamine released by mast cells → vasodilation and leaky capillaries → phagocytes arrive
options.C: Phagocytes arrive → histamine released → capillaries narrow
options.D: Interferon released → mast cells divide → swelling

questions.explanation: Mast cells release histamine, which widens arterioles and makes capillaries leaky, letting phagocytes and proteins reach the site. Option A is tempting, but antibodies are part of the slower adaptive response, not the start of inflammation.

questions.prompt: Natural killer cells recognise target cells mainly because the targets

options.A: display a specific antigen on MHC II.
options.C: have reduced MHC class I on their surface.

questions.explanation: NK cells are innate and non-specific; they detect stressed cells with reduced MHC I, as in many virus-infected and cancer cells. Option A is tempting, but recognising a specific antigen is how cytotoxic T cells work.

questions.prompt: Why does a person who had chickenpox as a child usually not get sick when exposed again?

options.A: Antibodies from the first infection stay in the blood at high levels forever.
options.B: Memory B and T cells produce a faster, larger secondary response.
options.C: The innate system has learned to recognise the virus.
options.D: The virus cannot enter the body a second time.

questions.explanation: Memory cells made during the first infection quickly expand and respond, so the pathogen is cleared before symptoms appear. Option A is tempting, but antibody levels fall after an infection; it is memory cells that last.

questions.prompt: A snakebite victim is given antivenom. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Antivenom contains ready-made antibodies given by injection, so it is artificial and passive, with no memory cells formed. Option B is tempting because it is a medical injection, but the person's own immune system did not make the antibodies.

questions.prompt: In hybridoma technology, plasma cells are fused with myeloma cells because myeloma cells

options.D: stop the mouse rejecting the antibody.

questions.explanation: Plasma cells make the antibody but do not keep dividing in culture; myeloma cells contribute the ability to divide indefinitely. Option B is tempting, but the antibody comes from the plasma cell.

questions.prompt: In a population of 200 beetles, 72 are BB, 96 are Bb and 32 are bb. What is the frequency of allele b?
questions.explanation: Copies of b = 96 + (2 × 32) = 160. Total alleles = 2 × 200 = 400. Frequency = 160 ÷ 400 = 0.40. Option A (0.16) is the proportion of bb individuals (32 ÷ 200), not the allele frequency.

questions.prompt: A storm kills 90% of a lizard population on an island at random. The survivors have lower genetic diversity. This is an example of
questions.explanation: A sudden random crash in population size is a bottleneck, a type of genetic drift. Option A is tempting, but natural selection depends on traits affecting survival; here survival was random. The founder effect involves a small group starting a new population elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Two populations of frogs live in the same pond, but one breeds in spring and the other in autumn. This isolating mechanism is
questions.explanation: Breeding at different times of year is temporal isolation, which stops mating before a zygote forms. Option B is tempting because breeding is a behaviour, but the key difference here is timing.

questions.prompt: A fossil bone contains 1/8 of the carbon-14 found in living organisms. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years. What is its approximate age?
questions.explanation: 1 → 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8 is 3 half-lives. Age = 3 × 5730 = 17 190 years. Option B (2 half-lives) is a common counting slip; option D comes from multiplying by 8 instead of counting halvings.

questions.prompt: Species P and Q differ by 4 amino acids in a protein, P and R by 12, and Q and R by 11. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: R is more closely related to P than to Q.
options.B: P and Q share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either does with R.
options.C: All three species are equally related.
options.D: R is the ancestor of P and Q.

questions.explanation: The fewest differences (4) are between P and Q, so they shared a common ancestor most recently. Option D is tempting, but living species cannot be ancestors of other living species; R simply branched off earlier.
